On a region with strict top-$K$ score margins, the discrete assignment fractions $f_i$ are constant. Write $z_i(x)=r_i^\top x$ and $p_i(x)=e^{z_i(x)}/\sum_\ell e^{z_\ell(x)}$. The softmax derivative gives the token coefficient and batch gradient
$$\beta_j(x)=\frac NBp_j(x)\left(f_j-\sum_i f_ip_i(x)\right),\qquad \nabla_{r_j}\mathcal L_{\mathrm{balance}}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal B}\beta_j(x)x.$$
First take $N=2$, $K=1$, $B=2$, tokens $x^{(1)}=(1,0)^\top$, $x^{(2)}=(0,1)^\top$, and router vectors $r_1=(\log3,0)^\top$, $r_2=(0,\log3)^\top$. Their probabilities are $(3/4,1/4)$ and $(1/4,3/4)$. The universal claim also fails with unequal loads. Take $N=4$, $K=1$ and ten tokens with probabilities
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{tokens}&(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)&\text{selected expert}\\\hline
1&(0.25,0.55,0.15,0.05)&2\\
2&(0.64,0.19,0.11,0.06)&1\\
3&(0.11,0.64,0.19,0.06)&2\\
4,5,6&(0.06,0.11,0.64,0.19)&3\\
7,8,9,10&(0.06,0.11,0.19,0.64)&4
\end{array}$$
Every row is positive and has distinct entries, and every expert is selected. These probabilities are realized by nonzero tokens $x^{(t)}=e_t\in\mathbb R^{10}$ and router coordinates $(r_j)_t=\log p_j(x^{(t)})$. The resulting loads are $f=(1,2,3,4)/10$. For token $1$,
$$\sum_i f_ip_i=0.1(0.25)+0.2(0.55)+0.3(0.15)+0.4(0.05)=0.2=f_2.$$
Thus $\beta_2(x^{(1)})=0$, while this token's coefficients for experts $1,3,4$ are nonzero. This is an active balancing configuration with one zero coefficient, not a claim that unequal-load gradients generally vanish.
